raw_case_text:
In March 2023, a 43-year-old Chinese male presented to the fever clinic with a one-week history of fever (peak temperature 39.8  C) and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. He had no significant medical history and denied corticosteroid or immunosuppressive drug use. On admission, the patient's vital signs were as follows: pulse rate 119 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, blood pressure 112/69 mmHg, and body temperature 38.5C. Laboratory tests showed normal white blood cell count (6.72 x 109/L; reference range, 3.5-9.5 x 109/L) but elevated neutrophil ratio (77.5 %; reference range, 40-75 %) and C-reactive protein (78.9 mg/L; reference range, 0-8 mg/L), liver function tests were within normal limits: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (32IU/L, reference range, 9-50 IU/L), Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) (40 IU/L, reference range, 15-40 IU/L).
Following evaluation at the fever clinic, he was admitted to the infectious disease department. Laboratory results revealed a positive HIV antibody test, the Jiaxing Municipal Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Jiaxing CDC: responsible for disease surveillance and public health management at the municipal level) confirmed the positive result, further laboratory tests revealed a CD4 count (163.4 cells/muL, reference range, 324.60-1274.70 cells/muL) and viral load (153,270 copies/mL, reference range, < 20 copies/mL). Enhanced abdominal CT scan revealed low-density areas in the right lobe of the liver, with a CT value of approximately 30 Hounsfield Unit (HU) and peripheral ring enhancement observed after the administration of contrast material, suggestive of an abscess (Fig. 1, panel A).
The patient had a persistent high fever, prompting ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage of the hepatic abscess (PLAD), which yielded a large amount of pus. Bacterial culture of the drained fluid (aerobic and anaerobic) and pre-antibiotic blood cultures (four bottles: 2 aerobic, 2 anaerobic from bilateral arms; three positive: both aerobic, left anaerobic) identified Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serotype Typhi (abbreviated as Salmonella Typhi: identified by biochemical tests (API 20E) and confirmed via MALDI-TOF MS). Using broth microdilution (MIC) and Kirby-Bauer (zone diameter) methods per CLSI 2023 guidelines, the isolate demonstrated susceptibility to: ceftazidime (MIC <= 1 mug/mL), cefepime (MIC <= 1 mug/mL), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (MIC <= 1/19 mug/mL), piperacillin-tazobactam (MIC 8 mug/mL), and aztreonam (MIC <= 1 mug/mL). Antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone 2000 mg every 24 h was initiated. However, despite continuous drainage of the liver abscess and targeted anti-Salmonella therapy, the patient continued to have a fever and gradually developed dyspnea. Chest and abdominal CT scans (on the 14th day of hospitalization) showed enlargement of the liver abscess and rupture into the pleural space (Fig. 1, panel B).
Further inquiry into his medical history revealed that the patient had a history of diarrhea and abdominal pain two months before presentation, which resolved spontaneously without treatment, and He originated from an amebiasis-endemic region in China and denied special social history.
Unfortunately, no hospitals or laboratories in southern China currently offer amoebic serological testing. Given the patient's pleuropulmonary involvement and CT findings suggestive of abscess rupture into the pleural space, an ultrasound-guided thoracentesis was performed (on the 14th day of hospitalization), which yielded 1500 mL of a "fish sauce-like" fluid, on the 16th day of hospitalization, mNGS of both pleural and liver abscess drainage fluids detected sequences of Entamoeba histolytica. Additionally, mNGS of the liver abscess drainage fluid revealed sequences of Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serotype Typhi (abbreviated as Salmonella Typhi) and Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serotype Typhimurium (abbreviated as Salmonella Typhimurium), then, rapid wet mount microscopic examination of additional liver drainage from drainage tubes fluid revealed unicellular organisms with pseudopods, suggestive of amoebic trophozoites (Fig. 1, panel C)
Combining findings from microscopic examination of the drainage fluid, microbiological culture, radiological imaging, and mNGS results, the diagnosis was confirmed as an amoebic liver abscess complicated by concurrent Salmonella Typhi and Salmonella Typhimurium bacterial liver abscesses. Although gastrointestinal endoscopy was recommended by the medical team due to the patient's prior intestinal symptoms, the patient declined further evaluation. However, the possibility of intestinal amoebic infection could not be ruled out. Consequently, the patient was treated with a 10-day regimen of metronidazole (750 mg every 8 h), 26-day ceftriaxone (2000 mg once daily), and paromomycin (500 mg three times daily, initiated 16 days after admission for a 10-day course.) to eradicate cysts in the intestinal lumen.
After treatment, the patient's symptoms resolved, and he was discharged in stable condition. Based on the antibiotic susceptibility testing of the Salmonella Typhi isolate from the aspirate culture, the patient continued oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for four weeks after discharge until inflammatory markers normalized completely and follow-up imaging confirmed complete resolution of the abscess.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old male presented with a 1-week history of high fever (peaking at 39.8 °C) and right upper quadrant abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In March 2023, the patient developed high fevers peaking at 39.8 °C and right upper quadrant abdominal pain of 1 week duration. Two months prior to presentation, he had an episode of diarrhea and abdominal pain that resolved spontaneously without medical intervention. He developed progressive dyspnea during the second week of hospitalization.
subjective.past_medical_history: No known chronic medical illnesses. Denied corticosteroid or immunosuppressive medication use. Originates from an amebiasis-endemic region of China. No significant social history.
subjective.review_of_systems: High fevers, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, dyspnea. Prior transient diarrhea and abdominal pain 2 months ago.

objective.physical_examination: Pulse rate 119 bpm, respiratory rate 18 bpm, blood pressure 112/69 mmHg, and body temperature 38.5 °C. Systemic examination findings not otherwise specified.
objective.routine_investigations: Body temperature 38.5 °C, pulse rate 119 bpm, BP 112/69 mmHg, RR 18 bpm. White blood cell count 6.72 x 10^9/L (reference range 3.5-9.5 x 10^9/L), neutrophil ratio 77.5% (40-75%), C-reactive protein 78.9 mg/L (0-8 mg/L), ALT 32 IU/L (9-50 IU/L), AST 40 IU/L (15-40 IU/L). Positive HIV antibody test confirmed by municipal CDC, CD4+ T-cell count 163.4 cells/muL (324.60-1274.70 cells/muL), and HIV viral load 153,270 copies/mL (<20 copies/mL).
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated low-density lesions in the right hepatic lobe (~30 Hounsfield Units) with peripheral ring enhancement, consistent with liver abscess. Repeat chest and abdominal CT on hospital day 14 revealed abscess enlargement with rupture through the diaphragm into the pleural space. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous liver abscess drainage (PLAD) yielded copious purulent fluid. Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis on hospital day 14 yielded 1500 mL of 'fish sauce-like' pleural fluid. Rapid wet mount microscopic examination of liver aspirate showed motile unicellular organisms with pseudopodia characteristic of amoebic trophozoites.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Amebic liver abscess complicated by concurrent Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serotype Typhi and Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serotype Typhimurium pyogenic co-infection, with secondary transdiaphragmatic rupture into the pleural space (empyema), in a patient with newly diagnosed HIV/AIDS (CD4 count 163.4 cells/muL). Pre-antibiotic blood cultures (3 of 4 bottles positive) and drained hepatic abscess fluid grew Salmonella Typhi (identified by API 20E and confirmed via MALDI-TOF MS). Broth microdilution and disc diffusion demonstrated susceptibility to ceftazidime (MIC <= 1 mug/mL), cefepime (MIC <= 1 mug/mL), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (MIC <= 1/19 mug/mL), piperacillin-tazobactam (MIC 8 mug/mL), and aztreonam (MIC <= 1 mug/mL). Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of pleural and liver fluids detected Entamoeba histolytica; liver fluid mNGS also identified S. Typhi and S. Typhimurium sequences.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with continuous catheter drainage, IV ceftriaxone 2000 mg every 24 hours for 26 days, metronidazole 750 mg every 8 hours for 10 days, and luminal cyst eradication with paromomycin 500 mg three times daily for 10 days (started on day 16). Discharged in stable condition to complete a 4-week course of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, achieving complete clinical recovery, normalization of inflammatory markers, and radiographic resolution of the abscess.
